html:
The Tashkent Metro, opened in November 1977, was the first underground railway in Central Asia and the seventh in the Soviet Union. It was built after the Tashkent earthquake of 1966 wrecked the old centre and the city was rebuilt as a Soviet showpiece.

Because Tashkent sits in an earthquake zone, the tunnels and stations were built to withstand strong shocks. Each station has its own theme, decorated with marble, granite, ceramics and chandeliers: Kosmonavtlar honours the cosmonauts, and Alisher Navoiy the classical poet, with domes in Central Asian style. Like the Moscow Metro, it was meant as a palace for the people.

Photography inside was banned for decades, partly because the system doubled as a shelter in case of nuclear war; the ban was lifted in 2018. The network now has four lines and about 50 stations, and it carries over 280 million passengers a year in the capital of Uzbekistan.
